abstract.t: The Agent Mailbox Access Protocol (AMAP) is a wire contract, carried over a filesystem namespace, between an untrusted per-agent connector and a trusted, credentialed mail runtime. It gives a sandboxed AI agent the ability to send and receive email through a runtime that does not trust it: every outbound message begins as an inert request file that the runtime copies into private staging, validates independently, and applies policy to before anything is transmitted, and every inbound message is authenticated and screened by the runtime before a notice describing it appears in the agent's namespace. This document specifies the directory layout and its filesystem obligations — ownership, write and delete rights, and the path, symlink, and concurrency discipline a runtime observes; the JSON message shapes for submit requests, results, deliver notices, spooled message bodies, and an optional binding record; the correlation and versioning rules, including a direction-aware unknown-member tolerance rule; and two conformance classes. AMAP is deliberately not a mail protocol: it neither defines nor replaces SMTP, IMAP, or provider-side infrastructure, and composes with them rather than displacing them. Its single design center is that no security property depends on the agent — or on the connector speaking for it — behaving correctly.

Naming. This protocol was called AMP ("Agent Mailbox Protocol") until 2026-09-15. It was renamed because AMP collides with the IETF DTN working group's adopted draft-ietf-dtn-amp. The filename of this draft is unchanged at this document version; the schema identifiers moved with the name (Change Log, 3.1.0).

section.name: Introduction — Motivation and Problem Statement
section.t: AI agents increasingly need email. They are tasked over it, they return results over it, and they correspond over it with people and with systems that speak no other protocol. An agent is nonetheless an untrusted process: it can be prompt-injected by the very content it is asked to read, it can be defective, and it can be compromised outright. Granting such a process email capability directly is dangerous along three concrete axes.

Inbound. Delivered mail is untrusted content routed directly into the agent's reasoning. A message body, a subject line, a sender display name, or an attachment filename can carry instructions the agent was never meant to follow. The delivery path is therefore an injection vector by construction, and no amount of care inside the agent removes that property.

Outbound. An agent that can send mail can exfiltrate anything it has read, to any address it chooses, and can do so under an identity that recipients associate with its operator. Outbound mail is simultaneously a data-loss channel and an impersonation channel.

Credentials and identity. Any mailbox credential, API token, or send endpoint held inside the agent's sandbox can be read, copied, or abused by whatever compromises the agent. Worse, an agent holding a credential has no identity of its own that a recipient — or its own operator — can verify independently of that credential.

section.name: Why the existing options are insufficient
section.t: Handing the agent mailbox credentials, or a mail-send API, makes the agent a trusted participant in the mail system. That is precisely the wrong posture for a component whose defining risk is that it may be compromised: the trust must be withdrawn exactly when it is least possible to detect that it should be. Wrapping the credential in a helper process that the agent calls does not change the analysis by itself, because a callable send capability is still a capability the agent holds; what matters is whether the capability crosses the boundary at all.

The common alternative is per-deployment glue: a bespoke script or service wired between one agent harness and one mail system. Such glue may even be correct, but it produces no reviewable contract, no interoperability, and no shared conformance bar. Nothing tells a second implementer what the first one guarantees, and nothing tells either of them what a third-party reviewer should check.

Adjacent agent protocols do not fill the gap, because they are solving a different problem: integration and interoperation among credentialed participants, rather than isolation of an untrusted one. positions AMAP against that landscape in detail.

section.name: The approach
section.t: AMAP interposes a trusted runtime between the agent and the mail system. The runtime holds every credential, owns the agent's sending identity, and makes every policy decision. The agent interacts with the runtime only through a channel that carries no capability: it writes an inert request file into a directory, and the runtime — independently, on its own schedule, over its own private copy of those bytes — decides what, if anything, happens next. In the other direction the runtime authenticates and screens mail before writing a notice describing it into the agent's namespace, and withholds the bytes of anything it will not vouch for.
The payoff, which the rest of this document formalizes, is the load-bearing invariant:

li.t: No security property depends on the agent — or on the connector speaking for it — behaving correctly. Enforcement is entirely runtime-side. A compromised agent or connector can at most write a well-formed request that the runtime then refuses.

section.t: AMAP is the wire contract at exactly that trust boundary, and is deliberately owned by neither side of it. That ownership choice is what allows a runtime and a connector built by different parties, on different schedules, to interoperate and to co-evolve against a versioned contract with an offline conformance suite.

section.name: Why a filesystem namespace rather than an API, RPC, or queue
section.t: The medium is the boundary. An API, an RPC endpoint, or a message queue is a live capability: something the agent invokes, whose invocation is itself the grant. Its security therefore rests on authenticating and authorizing each call, on the client library behaving, and on the transport being what it claims to be. A file written into a directory grants nothing at all. It has no callee, no session, and no side effect until a separate, trusted process chooses to read it — at a time of that process's choosing, into memory of its own, under validation of its own. The runtime is free to ignore the file, to refuse it, to hold it for human review, or to consume it and answer with a verdict. develops this point, along with the obligations it puts on the runtime in exchange.

list.t: Capability-free isolation. The channel available to an untrusted agent grants no send capability, no credential, and no reach outside its own namespace.
Vendor-neutral interoperability. A runtime and a connector built independently interoperate because both are built against this contract rather than against each other.

Versioned co-evolution with offline conformance. Either side proves conformance against a fixture suite with no counterpart present, and version changes are deliberate, legible, and fail closed rather than silent.
Composition with real email. Interactions remain federated, of-record, and human-inclusive, rather than confined to a closed agent-only channel.
Portability across agent runtimes. Nothing in the contract presumes a particular agent harness, language, or tool interface.

section.name: Non-goals

list.t: AMAP is not a mail transport. It neither defines nor replaces SMTP, IMAP, or any provider-side mail infrastructure. It describes what a runtime and a connector exchange locally; whatever the runtime does with a mail provider is out of scope.

AMAP is not an agent-to-agent networked RPC. The contract is local to one deployment's filesystem, between two components on either side of a single trust boundary. It defines no network protocol, no discovery mechanism, and no remote peer.

AMAP is not a policy language. What a runtime's policy decides — which recipients are permitted, which content is held for review, how a sender's standing is computed — is deliberately out of scope. The wire defines only the shapes of requests and verdicts, never the computation that produces them.

section.t: Every obligation in this document is grounded in what the contract actually provides. Where a capability is sketched but not in force, it is marked as such (), and where a property is a runtime obligation rather than a wire-verifiable fact, this document says so plainly ().

section.name: Conventions and Terminology
section.t: The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 when, and only when, they appear in all capitals, as shown here.
Every message defined by this document is a JSON text as defined by , encoded in UTF-8 . The schemas in through are written in the JSON Schema 2020-12 dialect .
Sections and subsections explicitly marked (informative) or (non-normative) carry no requirements; , , and the Change Log are the only such parts of this document.

list.t: Agent — the untrusted process whose email capability this protocol mediates. It holds no credential, has no send path of its own, and reaches the protocol only through its Connector. Nothing in this document places a requirement on the Agent, because no security property may depend on it.

Connector — the per-Agent component that speaks the Agent-side half of this contract: it writes Submit Requests, reads Results and Notices, and surfaces them to its Agent in whatever form its harness uses. It is semi-trusted at best; for the purpose of every security property in this document it is treated as untrusted, and the requirements placed on it are well-formedness and non-crashing obligations, never obligations another party's safety rests on.

Runtime — the trusted, credentialed, Agent-agnostic component that speaks the other half: it holds mail credentials, owns each Agent's identity, makes every policy decision, and is the only party that transmits or receives mail.

Volume — the runtime-owned filesystem tree carrying this protocol, containing one Namespace per Agent plus an optional Binding Record at its root. Its mount path is a deployment choice; this document writes <volume-root>/ for it and nothing in the protocol derives from its name. No implementation may depend on that name or any other.
Namespace — the per-Agent subtree <volume-root>/<agent-id>/, mounted into that Agent's sandbox. It is the unit of isolation and the sole authority for attributing an artifact to an Agent.
Submit Request — the Connector-authored artifact requesting that a message be sent (). It is inert: it carries no capability and effects nothing by existing.
Result — the Runtime-authored verdict for one consumed Submit Request ().
Notice (Deliver Notice) — the Runtime-authored artifact announcing that a message was delivered to the Agent's mailbox (). It is a pointer and summary, not the message.
Inbound Message — the Runtime-authored artifact carrying a delivered message's body text and headers, spooled under a Notice's identifier and fetched on demand ().
Binding Record — the optional, informational artifact at the Volume root naming which mailbox the Volume is bound to ().
Sidecar — attachment bytes stored beside a Submit Request or a Notice, in a directory named after that artifact, with each blob named by a 0-based ordinal.
Ordinal — the integer naming a Sidecar blob. It equals the index of the corresponding Descriptor in its array, and is the sole binding authority between a Descriptor and its bytes.

Descriptor — one entry in an attachments[] array, describing an attachment (its display filename, media type, size, and — depending on direction — digest, Disposition, or content reference). A Descriptor is metadata; it is never a path.
Disposition — the Runtime's assertion about an inbound attachment's handling: clean, stripped, quarantined, or unscanned ().
Staging — Runtime-private storage outside the Volume, unreachable from any Agent's mount, into which the Runtime copies Agent-authored bytes before acting on them ().

section.t: Where this document says an artifact is dropped, it means the consumer does not surface it to its Agent and does not act on it; where it says a consumer fails closed, it means the consumer refuses to process the artifact rather than proceeding on a partial or guessed interpretation.

section.name: Actors

texttable.c: mail-send credentials, Agent identity, policy, the record of what was sent
its own Namespace on the Volume; its Agent's input and output

section.t: The Runtime is trusted by construction: it is the party holding the credentials, and a compromise of it is a compromise of the mail capability itself. The Connector is the interesting case. It runs Agent-side, is reachable by whatever compromises the Agent, and is therefore treated as untrusted for every property that protects the Runtime, other Agents, or the outside world. Requirements this document places on a Connector fall into two distinct classes, and the difference matters when reading them:

list.t: Well-formedness and liveness obligations — emit valid documents, tolerate a missing artifact, do not crash on hostile input. A Connector that violates one harms itself and its own Agent, not any other party.

Obligations that protect an Agent from its own inbox — the untrusted-content posture of . These are necessarily Connector-implemented, because the Connector is the only component on the Agent's side of the boundary, and they are stated as such rather than as properties the Runtime relies on.

section.t: No requirement in this document places a Runtime-side, other-Agent-side, or outside-world safety property in a Connector's hands. Where an earlier reading of this contract appeared to do so — the Connector's obligation not to rewrite a published Submit Request — 's ingest-by-copy rule removes the dependency, leaving that obligation as pure well-formedness.

section.name: The load-bearing invariant

li.t: Invariant. No security property may depend on the Agent or the Connector behaving. Enforcement is entirely Runtime-side. A compromised Agent or Connector can at most write a well-formed request that the Runtime then refuses.

section.t: Everything else in this document is downstream of that sentence. It is why the Agent's declared identity is a cross-check rather than an attribution source (); why the Runtime re-derives every path from data it controls rather than from a file's contents (); why recipient policy is evaluated Runtime-side over the exact recipient set that will be transmitted to (); why the digest an Agent supplies for its own attachment bytes is an integrity aid and not a trust boundary (); and why the absence of bytes, rather than a flag inside a document, is the access gate on inbound attachments ().

The invariant also bounds what this document can promise. A wire contract cannot make a Runtime honest, and a fixture suite cannot observe a filesystem. states plainly which properties are wire-verifiable and which are Runtime obligations that a green conformance run does not prove.

section.name: Why a filesystem namespace
section.t: The Runtime mounts each Agent's Namespace into that Agent's sandbox, and the Agent's entire protocol surface is that directory. This is a deliberate choice of medium, with three consequences.

A file drop carries no capability. Writing a file invokes nothing. There is no callee to authenticate, no session to hijack, no method whose mere reachability is a grant. The request exists as bytes until a trusted process elects to look at them. Compare an API or queue, where the act of enqueuing is itself the privileged act and every security property depends on the authorization check in front of it being correct and unbypassable.

Isolation is structural rather than enforced by policy. A Connector scoped to <volume-root>/<agent-id>/ cannot name another Agent's Namespace at all. Attribution follows from where a file appeared, not from what the file says about itself, so spoofing attribution requires defeating the mount rather than lying in a JSON member.

The medium's costs are real and are paid explicitly. A shared filesystem between a trusted and an untrusted party is itself an attack surface: symlinks, directory swaps, special files, hard links, and unbounded sizes are all available to the untrusted side, and every path-based check the trusted side performs is racy against a concurrent rename. This document therefore does not treat "it is just a directory" as a simplification. states the path, open, copy, and concurrency discipline a Runtime observes in exchange for the medium's advantages, and revisits each as a threat.

section.name: Relationship to Other Agent Protocols (Informative)

t.em: This subsection is informative. It contains no requirements and creates no dependency on any external protocol. Nothing here claims that AMAP replaces, subsumes, or competes with any protocol named below.

section.t: AMAP occupies a narrow position: it is the local seam at a single trust boundary, where one side holds every credential and the other holds none. The adjacent protocols in the agent ecosystem sit at different layers, and the common question of "why not use one of them here" has a specific answer in each case.

Model Context Protocol (MCP) connects an agent host to tools and context through JSON-RPC servers. It is an integration interface: live capabilities are exposed across it and exercised by the agent through it. That makes MCP complementary to AMAP rather than an alternative. A Connector often surfaces AMAP's operations to its Agent through MCP, or through whatever tool interface its harness uses natively; AMAP is the capability-free seam sitting behind that surface. The contrast worth stating is exactly the one that motivates the two coexisting: an MCP-style interface grants live capability across the boundary it spans, while AMAP's channel deliberately grants none — the Agent-side surface can be as rich as the harness likes, because what crosses the trust boundary underneath it is an inert file. The current stable MCP specification revision is 2025-11-25; the protocol originated at Anthropic.

Agent2Agent (A2A) is networked agent-to-agent RPC between mutually authenticated services, with agent cards, tasks, and HTTP/SSE/JSON-RPC transport. It presumes both endpoints are credentialed participants that can authenticate to each other. AMAP's design center is the opposite: an untrusted agent that holds no credentials at all, with enforcement placed entirely on the trusted side of a local boundary. The two are orthogonal, and compose without friction — an agent that speaks A2A to its peers can use AMAP for its mail capability, and neither protocol needs to know about the other. A2A is at v1.0 (v1.0.1, May 2026); it originated at Google and has been hosted as a Linux Foundation project since June 2025.
The two protocols abbreviated "ACP" are not the same protocol, and the collision is worth disambiguating in a document a reviewer may arrive at with one of them in mind.

list.t: The Agent Communication Protocol (IBM/BeeAI) is of historical interest here: it merged into A2A under the Linux Foundation, announced in August 2025, with its repository archived .

The Agent Client Protocol is a distinct and currently active protocol at a different layer — an interface between a host or editor and an agent — originated by Zed Industries. It is unrelated to the merged Agent Communication Protocol and unrelated to AMAP.

section.name: Volume Layout
section.t: The Runtime owns the Volume and mounts each Agent's Namespace into that Agent's sandbox. A Connector has access only within its own <agent-id>/, and only to the paths below. Within that Namespace, write access may be narrower still: the inbound/ subtree is Runtime-owned and MAY be mounted read-only.

The Volume root's own name is a deployment choice and is not part of this protocol — nothing derives from it, and no implementation may depend on it. <volume-root>/ below stands for whatever a deployment calls it.

(S7.2) notices/processed/ # OPTIONAL - connector archive, # writable-inbound deployments only messages/notice-<id>.json # runtime -> agent: full message cursor.json # runtime: inbound poll cursor audit/ log.jsonl # runtime: append-only action log

section.t: There is exactly one inbound Sidecar directory — inbound/notices/<notice-id>.attachments/ — and both a Deliver Notice's and an Inbound Message's content_ref resolve there. No second, message-specific Sidecar directory exists.

section.name: Obligations
section.t: Attribution by Namespace. <agent-id> is Runtime-assigned and never self-declared. Attribution is the Namespace a file arrived in, never an agent_id member inside the file; that member is a cross-check only, never the source of truth. A Runtime MUST reject a Submit Request whose agent_id, when present, does not match the Namespace it was found in, and MUST NOT use that member to attribute the request.
Isolation is structural. A Connector scoped to <agent-id>/ cannot read another Agent's drafts or Notices.
All writes are atomic. Every artifact in the tree above is published by writing a .tmp sibling and then renaming it into place (os.replace or the equivalent). Readers MUST ignore *.tmp entries.

Single writer, single drainer. At any moment a Namespace has exactly one Connector instance writing outbound/ and exactly one Runtime instance draining it. Every concurrency-sensitive rule in this document — the atomic .tmp-then-rename discipline above, the commit sentinel below, and the derivation of req_id from max(pending, processed, results) + 1 () — is sound only under that assumption and provides no mutual exclusion of its own. Each side MUST ensure single-instance operation over a Namespace by a mechanism outside this protocol, such as an OS-level lock held for the process lifetime. A Runtime MUST NOT run two concurrent drains of one Namespace, and a Connector MUST NOT run two concurrent writers into one. Behavior under violation is unspecified: duplicated delivery, clobbered published requests, and false verdicts are all reachable.

Filename identifiers are the authority for paths. An identifier taken from a file's contents — a req_id member in a request body, for instance — MUST NOT determine a write path. The Runtime derives identifiers from the validated filename, on a restricted character set. (This obligation follows from a confirmed exploit in an early implementation: trusting a file's own contents, rather than its validated filename, to name a write path.)

Write-side path discipline. Every write, rename, directory creation, or archive move into or within a Namespace MUST satisfy all three of the following conjunctively. Each closes a distinct gap the other two leave open, and none is sufficient alone.

list.t: (a) Full parent-chain pinning. The write resolves its full parent chain through pinned directory descriptors from the Namespace root — openat, mkdirat, renameat off a descriptor the Runtime opened once per Namespace — never by re-resolving a path string for the act itself. A path-based containment check followed by a path-based act is a race, not a check: the parent directory the check inspected and the parent directory the act touches are not guaranteed to be the same object, because the Agent can swap a parent directory for a symlink in between. Applying a no-follow flag to the final path component alone does not close this gap — it constrains only the last component, not a swapped parent — and rename and directory-creation calls have no no-follow equivalent at all, so a bare "writes do not follow symlinks" requirement is not sufficient on its own.

(b) No-follow while building the chain. Each directory component that goes into that parent chain MUST itself have been opened with O_NOFOLLOW|O_DIRECTORY at the moment it was added to the pinned chain. A descriptor counts as pinned only if the open that produced it refused to follow a symlink at that step. Requirement (a) without this is equally insufficient, and the gap is the symmetric one: nothing otherwise stops the Runtime from acquiring a "pinned" descriptor by following an Agent-planted symlink in the first place — the Agent replaces a Namespace subdirectory with a symlink before the Runtime's once-per-Namespace open, or before a later re-open after a restart — and a descriptor obtained that way is pinned to the wrong object, so every write built off it inherits the redirection no matter how faithfully (a) is followed from there.

(c) Non-following final component. The final path component MUST NOT be followed if a symlink exists at that name: the open MUST carry O_NOFOLLOW and MUST fail closed on ELOOP rather than writing through whatever the name currently resolves to. Two cases differ in what else they require, and both are covered:
A newly created file — the .tmp sibling the atomicity rule above already requires, and any Sidecar blob — MUST additionally be created with O_EXCL (O_WRONLY|O_CREAT|O_EXCL, never O_TRUNC in place of O_EXCL), failing closed on EEXIST. An append-mode or directory-creating write that has no .tmp sibling — audit/log.jsonl is the case this document names — cannot use O_EXCL, because the target legitimately already exists. It MUST instead open with O_NOFOLLOW|O_APPEND|O_NONBLOCK (or use mkdirat with the parent pinned per (b)), MUST NOT block on a special file, and MUST verify through the resulting descriptor (fstat, never a pre-open stat) that the object is a regular file it may append to; it SHOULD refuse a target whose link count exceeds 1. The non-blocking open is load-bearing and is not a performance concern: O_NOFOLLOW does not apply to a FIFO — a FIFO is not a symlink — and opening one for writing blocks until a reader appears, so without O_NONBLOCK the fstat is never reached and an Agent that plants a FIFO at this name stalls the drain indefinitely. The first branch's O_EXCL refuses that case on its own; the second branch has no O_EXCL to lean on and states it explicitly. Requiring O_EXCL in the second branch would forbid appending to an existing log at all; requiring nothing there would leave the one write this document names that has no .tmp sibling unprotected.
Requirement (c) is needed in both of its branches because an Agent can pre-plant a symlink at a filename the Runtime is about to write. req_id is Agent-chosen, and every Runtime-written filename in the layout tree above — results/<id>.json, the .tmp sibling of processed/req-<id>.json, inbound/notices/notice-<id>.json, inbound/messages/notice-<id>.json, audit/log.jsonl — is reachable to an Agent that can predict or observe it. Absent (c), such a name gets its bytes written through the planted symlink with the Runtime's own privileges, even though the parent chain that reached the containing directory was itself correctly pinned under (a) and (b). This discipline governs every Runtime-side write named in the layout tree, not only the initial consumption of an Agent-authored artifact.

section.t: Read-side discipline. The same rule applied to reads. When the Runtime opens any path the Agent can influence — every req-<id>.json, every Sidecar ordinal, and, in a deployment that leaves inbound/ writable, anything it later reads back from there — it MUST open without following symbolic links at any component (per-component O_NOFOLLOW, or an equivalently pinned directory-descriptor walk from the Namespace root, matching the write-side rule above), MUST NOT block on a special file (a non-blocking open), MUST verify that the opened object is a regular file through the open descriptor (fstat and an S_ISREG test — never a pre-open stat, which is a race), SHOULD refuse a file whose link count exceeds 1, and MUST enforce a deployment-configured per-file size cap (a bounded read) and a per-request Sidecar count cap. The too_large value in the Result vocabulary () presumes that cap: enforcing one is an obligation, not an option.

A Connector's one Agent-influenceable read path — resolving a notice_id to inbound/messages/notice-<id>.json — MUST be built only from a pattern-validated notice_id (the schemas pin the pattern) and MUST confine resolution to the Connector's own inbound/ tree ().

Sidecar ordinal binding. Sidecar blobs are named by Runtime-assigned 0-based ordinals equal to the Descriptor's array index, which is the sole binding authority. Nothing else names a blob; a Descriptor's filename is display-only and is never a path.

Commit sentinel. All Sidecar bytes are written — .tmp sibling, then rename — before req-<id>.json; the JSON file's presence is the only publish signal. The Runtime MUST verify that every referenced ordinal exists and MUST re-verify size and digest before acting on the request, against the snapshot it took at ingest (below), never against the live path.

Inbound Sidecar directories are keyed on the Runtime-minted notice identifier, never the provider message.id. The provider identifier is external and is not character-set-safe; using one as a path component was a confirmed exploit path in an early implementation. The same rule extends to the body artifact: inbound/messages/notice-<id>.json is keyed on the notice identifier, never on message.id. Inbound bytes are published only at inbound/notices/<notice-id>.attachments/<index>, the single Sidecar directory named in the layout tree.
Runtime-private Staging lives outside the mounted Volume — at a path the Agent's mount cannot reach at all.

Ingest by copy. Before validating, evaluating policy on, or composing from any Agent-authored artifact — req-<id>.json and every Sidecar ordinal — the Runtime MUST copy the bytes into Runtime-private Staging and MUST act only on that private copy. All checks — schema validation, recipient policy, size and sha256 verification — and all message composition MUST run over that snapshot, and the Runtime MUST NOT re-read any Agent-writable path after a decision that depends on its content. Verify-then-use against a live Agent-writable path is a race, not a check.

This obligation is what makes the Connector's "MUST NOT delete or rewrite a published request" () a pure well-formedness rule: a Runtime MAY treat an observed post-publish change as malformed, but no safety property depends on the Connector honoring immutability — which is what the invariant of requires. (This governs the properties that protect the Runtime, other Agents, and the outside world. Obligations that protect an Agent from its own inbox are necessarily Connector-implemented and are stated as such, not as properties the Runtime relies on a Connector for.)
Byte-absence is the gate. The Runtime MUST NOT place non-clean bytes in an Agent's Namespace. content_ref is the Runtime's access grant, present only for bytes it has published as clean ().

Tree rules. Every Runtime-owned inbound-class tree is an origin class: a consumer derives the class of a document from the tree it was read from, and never from any member of the document. notice_id uniqueness is per tree, and where a tree has more than one writer each MUST mint so that cross-writer collision is negligible — at least 128 bits of entropy under the identifier character set, or a writer-specific prefix — and a consumer keying state across trees MUST include the tree in that key. content_ref resolves only within the notices/ directory of the tree the enclosing document was read from. Write authority per tree is distinct and MUST be structurally enforced, never by configuration the writer itself reads. inbound/ is the one tree this document defines; a profile MAY define others.

Inbound is Runtime-owned, and read-only is a valid posture. The inbound/ tree is Runtime-owned end to end. A Runtime MAY expose it to the sandbox read-only — for instance as a read-only mount, which is the mechanism that actually makes a delivered Notice unforgeable, since file permission bits do not bind a same-uid Agent, which can change a mode it owns. A Connector MUST NOT require write access anywhere under inbound/: it MUST start, relay Notices, and resolve bodies when every write, rename, and directory creation under inbound/ fails. inbound/notices/processed/ is OPTIONAL — a conventional archive location a Connector MAY use only where a deployment leaves inbound writable; nothing on either side may depend on its existence or its contents.

Consumption tracking is Connector-private. How a Connector records which Notices it has already relayed to its Agent is Connector-private state, outside this protocol. Such state lives in the Connector's own storage outside the Volume, or in Connector-owned paths under outbound/ not enumerated in the layout tree — which MUST NOT use the req- prefix, reserved for Submit Requests and their Sidecars, so that a Runtime's scan of the drop-box never encounters Connector-private state. Either way, the Runtime neither reads nor relies on it. A seam-visible consumption signal is deliberately not specified at this document version; records the reasoning.

Outbound extension space (v3.1.0 DRAFT). outbound/ext/<name>/ is a Connector-owned side channel, one directory per <name>, that a Runtime MAY read by out-of-band agreement. <name> is a stable Connector id: the Connector chooses it once, and it MUST NOT change when the Connector's repository, package, or deployment is renamed or moved. A Runtime that reads the directory MUST treat <name> as opaque — it is an identifier, never a name to be parsed, resolved, or matched against a repository or path. This document specifies no shape for anything under it; it lies outside the req- prefix the Runtime scans, and nothing security-relevant may be built on it. Its first use is a Connector's per-Notice outcome file, written by the receiving Agent's own uid and therefore forgeable by construction. An outcome is a statement by the receiving side about what it did with a Notice; a party MUST NOT treat an outcome as proof of delivery or of non-delivery, and the Runtime's own delivery record is authoritative over it (). There is deliberately no inbound extension space: an inbound tree is a Runtime assertion about origin, and a Connector cannot know what a vendor-named assertion means.

section.name: Deletion rights
section.t: This table names who may delete each artifact. It is permissive: a party exercising a right it already effectively had — a Runtime deleting from its own Runtime-owned tree, for instance — changes nothing about what conformant behavior looks like.

texttable.c: Consumption — the move to processed/, or deletion once the Result is written. The Connector MUST NOT delete or rewrite a published request; the JSON file's presence is the commit signal, and un-publishing is unspecified.
Runtime at will; Connector after reading the matching Result

The Runtime's own archive. Caveat: derives req_id from max(pending, processed, results) + 1, so a Connector that deletes here (or in results/) MUST preserve req_id monotonicity by other durable means, such as its own counter. Correspondingly, a Runtime MUST NOT rely on processed/ contents as durable state (for deduplication, say) — the Connector may delete there, and the Runtime's own record lives outside this protocol.
Connector, once read; Runtime by retention
No signal in this protocol tells the Runtime that a Connector has read a verdict, so Runtime-side deletion SHOULD be age-based and generous: a Result deleted before it is read is a lost verdict.
inbound/notices/notice-<id>.json, inbound/messages/notice-<id>.json, and their .attachments/ Sidecar directories
Runtime only. Where a deployment leaves inbound writable, the Connector MAY move or delete per the optional processed/ convention, but MUST NOT depend on the ability.

Runtime retention policy. Absent a seam-visible consumption signal (), retention MUST be conservative and age-based. A Connector already tolerates the disappearance of these artifacts: a read against a missing one returns "not resolved" ().

section.name: Outbound: Submit Request
section.t: An Agent's only outbound action is dropping an inert request file into its Namespace. The file carries no send capability; the Runtime enforces policy before anything leaves.

A Submit Request is written to <volume-root>/<agent-id>/outbound/req-<id>.json as a JSON text . Its Sidecar bytes, if any, are written first, into req-<id>.attachments/, one blob per Descriptor, named by that Descriptor's 0-based array index (, commit sentinel).

figure.title: draft/examples/submit-request.json (illustrative — not a fixture)

{ "contract_version": "2", "req_id": "00000001", "agent_id": "agent.research", "ts": "2026-07-20T04:10:56Z", "in_reply_to": "1721457600000000000-4242", "draft": { "to": ["owner@example.com"], "cc": [], "subject": "Run report", "body_text": "The run finished; details below.", "reply_to_message_id": null, "attachments": [ { "filename": "report.pdf", "media_type": "application/pdf", "size_bytes": 48213, "sha256": "970e441b6c4ecd37abf2541e1276c680bdec8481cef9368ff\ 1d010fd6b784b07" } ] } }

section.t: The normative shape is . The Submit Request envelope is closed: additionalProperties is false at every level, and a Runtime MUST reject a request carrying any unrecognized member. explains why this direction is closed while the Runtime-authored artifacts are open.

list.t: contract_version (REQUIRED) is the wire major version, the string "2" at this document version. A Runtime MUST check it before schema validation and MUST fail closed on an absent, lower, or higher major ().

req_id (REQUIRED) is monotonic per Namespace and MUST NOT be reused across the drop-box's life; derive it from max(pending, processed, results) + 1. Reuse collides message identifiers and triggers provider-side idempotency deduplication. req_id is pinned to a filename-safe character set by the schema, but it is not the path authority: the Runtime derives the path identifier from the validated filename ().
agent_id (OPTIONAL), if present, MUST match the Namespace the request was found in, and a Runtime MUST reject a mismatch. It is never the attribution source ().
ts (OPTIONAL) is the Connector's timestamp for the request. It is Agent-authored and therefore advisory.

in_reply_to (OPTIONAL) correlates this request with prior inbound work. It carries either a Runtime-minted notice_id or a mail message identifier . It is a hint from an untrusted party and MUST NOT by itself widen what the request is permitted to do — the same posture fixes for task_id.
The Runtime derives the message identity and the From/Reply-To of the composed message itself; identity is Runtime-owned, and the Agent does not choose its sending identity.
draft.subject and draft.body_text are REQUIRED and MAY be empty strings. body_text is plain text; this document defines no alternative body representation at this version.

draft.reply_to_message_id (OPTIONAL, nullable) names the message this draft replies to, as an message identifier. It is composed directly into an In-Reply-To: header, which is why it carries a control-character pattern in the schema (below).

Recipient policy is a Runtime decision. The Agent's chosen draft.to and draft.cc are not inherently trusted. Allowlisting, task-counterpart binding, and any other recipient rule are evaluated Runtime-side. A populated allowlist plus a fresh recipient is an exfiltration surface that the Runtime, not the Connector, must close.

Recipient syntax and header-injection discipline. Each draft.to and draft.cc element is exactly one bare addr-spec: no display name, address list, quoted local part, comment, IP literal, or folding whitespace. The schema pins the pattern. This profile is deliberately narrower than , because those excluded forms are exactly what makes allowlist evaluation non-mechanical; internationalized (EAI/SMTPUTF8) addresses are out of scope at this version and may be added later. A Runtime MUST reject — with a top-level rejected Result — a request whose recipient entries do not parse under this profile, MUST evaluate recipient policy over exactly the recipient set it will transmit to, and MUST NOT transmit to any address not present in draft.to or draft.cc. Separately, a Runtime MUST NOT allow any Agent-authored string — subject, a recipient entry, an attachment filename, an attachment media_type, draft.reply_to_message_id, in_reply_to, agent_id, ts, or body_text where it abuts headers — to introduce a header boundary in the composed message. CR, LF, and NUL MUST be rejected or stripped before composition even where schema validation was bypassed upstream: the schema-level control-character patterns on subject, filename, media_type, reply_to_message_id, in_reply_to, agent_id, and ts are the first line of defense, not the only one. Two of those fields matter for a reason worth stating explicitly, because narrower schema coverage in an earlier revision of this protocol missed exactly them: reply_to_message_id and media_type are composed directly into headers — In-Reply-To: and a MIME part's Content-Type: respectively — rather than into a body or a display field.

draft.attachments[] (OPTIONAL) is an array of Descriptors, each carrying filename, media_type, size_bytes, and sha256. size_bytes and sha256 are REQUIRED on every Descriptor, computed by the Connector over the decoded bytes it wrote, with sha256 in lowercase hexadecimal. There is no outbound content_ref. The Runtime re-derives each Sidecar's path from req-<id> plus the Descriptor's array index, which is the sole binding authority; an Agent-supplied path string would be pure disagreement and attack surface, so it is absent from the schema entirely and additionalProperties: false rejects it. attachments: [] is valid and is equivalent to the member being absent; the Sidecar directory MUST then be absent. sha256 here is an integrity and deduplication aid, not an outbound trust boundary: the Agent controls both the bytes and the hash, so a mismatch catches corruption, never a hostile Agent. Its value to the Runtime is that it detects an inconsistent request, not that it authenticates one.

section.name: Outbound: Result
section.t: A Result is the Runtime's verdict for one consumed Submit Request, written to <volume-root>/<agent-id>/outbound/results/<id>.json.

figure.title: draft/examples/result.json (illustrative — not a fixture)

section.t: The normative shape is . The Result envelope is open: a consumer MUST tolerate members it does not recognize, at every level ().

list.t: The Runtime writes exactly one Result per Submit Request it consumes. A request the Runtime never consumes gets no Result, and no signal in this protocol distinguishes "not yet" from "never."

outcome (REQUIRED) is one of accepted, queued_for_human, or rejected. This is a closed vocabulary: it gates which processing path a document takes, so a consumer cannot safely treat an unrecognized value as opaque, and introducing a new value is a major change ().
Any policy miss — allowlist, rate limit, DLP hold, halt — MUST produce queued_for_human. Never a silent send; never a silent drop.
accepted means the provider accepted the message for relay. Downstream delivery or quarantine is out of the Runtime's hands and is surfaced later via an inbound delivery-status notification, if any.
detail (OPTIONAL, nullable) is human-readable text. It carries no machine semantics.

reason_code (OPTIONAL) records which policy path authorized or refused the request; human text stays in detail. A Runtime SHOULD set a reason on every Result, successes included. The suggested vocabulary — recipient_bound, allowlisted, no_verified_counterparty, recipient_not_allowlisted, dlp_hold, no_screener, halted, rate_limited, unsupported_contract_version — is extensible and not enum-locked in the schema. Two consumer obligations follow: a consumer MUST tolerate a reason_code it does not recognize, treating it as opaque and never as an error, and a consumer MUST NOT infer the outcome from it. outcome is the sole authoritative verdict; reason_code only explains which path produced it, and a Runtime may add codes at any time without a protocol change. unsupported_contract_version is the code a Runtime sets on the rejected Result it writes for a version-refused Submit Request ().
ts (OPTIONAL) is the Runtime-set, of-record time of the verdict, in ISO-8601 form.
recipients (OPTIONAL) records the recipient set the Runtime actually transmitted to.
message_id (OPTIONAL, nullable) is the message identifier the Runtime assigned to the composed message.
job_id (OPTIONAL, nullable) is a provider-side job identifier, opaque to this protocol.

attestation (OPTIONAL) is the identity stamp the Runtime applied to the outbound message. Its form is self-stamp or verifiable, distinguishing a stamp a stranger cannot verify from one that can be verified independently. A Connector surfaces an attestation; it never verifies one, which is a Runtime concern.

attachments[] (OPTIONAL) carries one diagnostic entry per submitted attachment: index, an outcome of accepted, dlp_held, rejected_type, or too_large, and an optional detail. index MUST equal the entry's own position in the array — contiguous, unique, and covering 0 through n-1 exactly once. Array position is the binding authority for attachments in both directions (). This constraint is not expressible in JSON Schema and is enforced by the conformance gate as a named post-check rather than by the schema (). Two paths, never conflated. A malformed attachment — a size or digest mismatch, a missing or extra Sidecar, a duplicate index — is not a policy decision: it fails the whole request with a top-level rejected. A policy hold — DLP, a disallowed type, a size cap, including a fail-closed hold when no screener is available — is queued_for_human. Per-attachment outcomes are diagnostic detail under one governing top-level outcome; they never license a partial send.

section.name: Inbound: Deliver Notice and Inbound Message
section.t: The Runtime writes one Deliver Notice per delivered message. Quarantined or unverified mail produces no Notice: it is logged Runtime-side and is never seen by the Agent. The Notice is a pointer and summary; the body is fetched on demand from a separate spooled artifact () and is untrusted content.

figure.title: draft/examples/deliver-notice.json (illustrative — not a fixture)
figure.sourcecode: { "contract_version": "2", "notice_id": "1721457600000000000-4242", "ts": "2026-07-20T04:00:00Z", "kind": "deliver", "message": { "id": "42", "from": "Alex Doe <owner@example.com>", "subject": "status?", "preview": "hey, how is the run going", "mailbox": "inbox", "task_id": "0f1e2d3c4b5a6978", "thread_id": "T-9182", "in_reply_to": "<20260719120000.7@example.com>", "references": ["<20260718090000.3@example.com>"], "sender_standing": "known", "provenance": "external", "verdict": { "auth": "dmarc-pass", "screen": "clean", "entitlement": "task-counterparty" }, "attachments": [ { "filename": "invoice.pdf", "media_type": "application/pdf", "size_bytes": 12345, "disposition": "unscanned" } ] } }

section.t: The normative shape is . The Deliver Notice envelope is open: a consumer MUST tolerate members it does not recognize, at every level ().

section.name: Field semantics and obligations
section.t: The drop rule. A Connector relays only deliver Notices. It MUST drop — not surface — a Notice that fails either of two independent checks, treating a failure of either one alone as sufficient grounds to drop:

list.t: Schema failure. The Notice fails validation against the deliver-notice schema () for any reason other than an unrecognized member. That single formulation covers a kind other than deliver, a missing required member, an enum violation on a closed vocabulary, a pattern violation (including a traversal or character-set violation in notice_id, or a shape violation in content_ref's own pattern), a conditional (allOf / if-then) violation, and a type violation alike, with no need to enumerate schema-failure categories separately. An unrecognized member is never grounds for a drop (); that is the one carve-out from "fails schema validation."

The content_ref index and prefix binding. A Notice can pass check 1 — every member individually well-shaped — and still carry an attachment Descriptor whose content_ref does not equal <notice_id>.attachments/<i> for its own 0-based array position i (): a mismatched trailing index, or a leading notice_id prefix pointing into a different Notice's Sidecar directory. A Connector MUST run this check independently of schema validation and MUST drop the Notice on failure exactly as it would a schema failure.

section.t: This is not a closure over schema validation. Check 2 binds two members of the same document — a Descriptor's content_ref against the enclosing document's own notice_id and against the Descriptor's own array position — against each other, which is not expressible in the JSON Schema vocabulary these schemas use . It therefore cannot be folded into "fails schema validation" no matter how the schema is phrased: it is a second, independent condition, not a special case of the first. The conformance suite enforces it as a named post-check and pins it with a fixture that is schema-valid on its own and fails only this check ().

A version refusal — an absent or non-matching contract_version major — is explicitly not part of this drop path. It is handled first and separately () as a distinct, logged outcome: a Connector checks the version before it ever reaches schema validation, so a version-refused Notice never falls into the drop rule at all.
A document with kind: "peer" found under inbound/notices/ fails check 1 against this schema, and is dropped the same way (, the peer-origin profile's cross-lock).

list.t: contract_version, notice_id, ts, kind, and message are REQUIRED. notice_id is Runtime-minted and is pinned by the schema to a character set that is safe as a path component and as a content_ref prefix.
Required members of message are id, from, subject, preview, and mailbox. The rest is enrichment ().
message.id is the provider's message identifier. It is external and not character-set-safe, and MUST NOT be used as a path component anywhere ().

message.from is attacker-controlled display data. Its display-name half is chosen freely by the sender — "security@yourbank.example <attacker@evil.example>" is a legal value — and it MUST NOT be used for any trust decision, nor rendered to a human or to an Agent as verified identity. Verified sender identity is only ever what the Runtime summarizes into sender_standing and verdict; it is never the from string itself.

Presentation obligations. A Connector that presents a message body to its Agent MUST convey two things, whatever words it uses: quoted or forwarded material inside the body carries no authority of its own — a message's authority extends to what its author wrote, never to what they relayed — and that an attachment's disposition is the Runtime's assertion about handling and not a scanner verdict, so a Connector MUST NOT imply that bytes have been screened and MUST NOT contradict the per-attachment status the Runtime published. A Connector MUST also convey that an attachment's filename and media_type are sender-chosen display strings on the mail tree; on a tree whose sender the Runtime authenticated it SHOULD, and MUST where the attachment was relayed rather than authored by that sender. On the mail tree a Connector MUST additionally convey that the sender is not authenticated beyond whatever standing the Runtime has already summarized — carried in sender_standing and verdict, named here as the locus and not as vocabulary to repeat to a reader — and that message.from is sender-chosen text. These are obligations about substance, not vocabulary: a Connector satisfies them with any wording its reader can act on without consulting this document, and they MUST be satisfiable by a literal string the Connector carries, requiring no lookup or computation when a body is presented.

The untrusted-content posture covers every sender-originated string in the Notice and in the spooled Inbound Message: message.from, subject, preview, body_text, references, attachment filename and media_type, and the Inbound Message's from, to, cc, and subject. This is not limited to the members called out individually here.

message.sender_standing (OPTIONAL) is an open, advisory vocabulary — known, agent-tier, first-contact, read-only, and others. How the values are computed is Runtime policy and out of scope; the wire fixes only today's known vocabulary, so that a Connector can tell its Agent "stranger," "agent," or "needs sign-off." A Connector MUST tolerate a value outside this list, treating it as opaque — never as grounds to drop the Notice — and a Runtime MAY add a value as a minor change ().

message.provenance (OPTIONAL) classifies the message source — external, internal, and others — so that a Runtime can route provenance-labelled screening. It is advisory metadata, like verdict, and never a license for an Agent to obey body content. It is likewise an open, advisory vocabulary: a Connector MUST tolerate a value outside this list, treating it as opaque, and MUST NOT drop the Notice on its account; a Runtime MAY add a value as a minor change.

message.verdict (OPTIONAL) carries the upstream authentication, screening, and entitlement results the Runtime consumed. A Connector treats it as advisory metadata, never as license for an Agent to obey body content. The object is open: unrecognized members inside it are tolerated, as they are everywhere else in this artifact.
message.thread_id, message.in_reply_to, and message.references (all OPTIONAL) carry provider and threading identity. They grant correlation, never trust ().
message.task_id (OPTIONAL) is Runtime-minted; states the obligations on it.

section.t: Direction and openness. This artifact is Runtime-authored, and its envelope is open at every level: a Connector MUST tolerate a member it does not recognize, in message or at the top level, and MUST NOT drop the Notice on that account. Emitting an unrecognized member remains Runtime non-conformance ().

section.name: Inbound attachment Descriptors
section.t: message.attachments[] (OPTIONAL) is an array of Descriptors carrying filename, media_type, and size_bytes — all REQUIRED — plus a REQUIRED disposition, and OPTIONAL sha256 and content_ref members gated on it.

disposition is the Runtime's assertion, not a scanner verdict. Its values are clean, stripped, quarantined, and unscanned, and the vocabulary is closed: it gates byte publication, so a new value would be a behavioral fork a consumer cannot treat as opaque, and introducing one is a major change (). On what basis a Runtime asserts clean is deliberately unspecified — a screening pipeline's pass in one deployment, a closed operator-supervised topology in another. That is Runtime policy and out of scope for the wire, the same posture sender_standing takes: the wire fixes the vocabulary, never the computation. The Runtime is trusted by construction (); the load-bearing invariant is that the Agent is not.

The counterpart obligation is equally plain: a Runtime that cannot make the determination MUST NOT assert clean. It emits unscanned — or stripped or quarantined where it made that decision — and publishes no bytes.

Byte publication and the access grant. A Runtime MAY publish an attachment's bytes at inbound/notices/<notice-id>.attachments/<index> only for a Descriptor it asserts disposition == "clean", and only then MAY it emit content_ref (a path of the form <notice-id>.attachments/<index>) and sha256. Byte-absence remains the gate () for anything not asserted clean. Exposing sha256 on a withheld item would be a confirmation oracle for no integrity value, which is why it is clean-gated too. Both conditionals are expressed in the schema.

The content_ref binding. content_ref's leading notice_id prefix MUST equal the enclosing document's own notice_id, and its trailing <index> MUST equal the Descriptor's own 0-based array index. The array index remains the sole binding authority (), and a consumer that resolves bytes MUST derive the path from the enclosing notice_id and the index — never trusting the content_ref string's own text as the path, since a Descriptor could otherwise point into another Notice's Sidecar directory. This is a wire-shaped, document-level obligation, enforced by the conformance gate as a named post-check () in the same way the Result-side attachments[i].index == i binding is.

A grant, never a directive. A consumer MUST tolerate a Descriptor whose bytes it does not resolve — relaying the Notice as usual — and MUST NOT treat the presence of content_ref as a requirement to fetch. A Connector that never dereferences content_ref remains fully conformant. A Connector MUST resolve published bytes only within its own Namespace's inbound/notices/ tree and MUST reject any content_ref that does not match the pinned pattern — the same confinement 's read-side discipline requires generally.

filename and media_type here are attacker-controlled, untrusted display strings. The untrusted-content posture extends to attachment Descriptors: a quarantined file named to look like an instruction is still an injection payload even with its bytes withheld. A clean assertion covers the bytes' screening disposition, never the truthfulness of these strings.
Inbound size_bytes is provider-declared and therefore advisory and untrusted — it comes from the provider's structure report, and is not Runtime-verified the way outbound size_bytes is.

MIME edges. filename is the / -decoded, Runtime-sanitized display string. An "attachment" is any part carrying Content-Disposition: attachment , or any named or non-inline text part — inline images and multipart/related parts count, which is the conservative reading of and . The declared media_type is display-only: the Runtime sniffs the bytes, and the sniffed type governs policy on the outbound gate.

section.name: The Inbound Message (body spool)
section.t: The Runtime spools the delivered body at <volume-root>/<agent-id>/inbound/messages/notice-<id>.json, keyed on the Runtime-minted notice identifier — never on the provider message.id, for the same confirmed-exploit reason given in .

figure.title: draft/examples/inbound-message.json (illustrative — not a fixture)
figure.sourcecode: { "contract_version": "2", "notice_id": "1721457600000000000-4242", "id": "42", "date": "Mon, 20 Jul 2026 04:00:00 +0000", "from": "Alex Doe <owner@example.com>", "to": "agent@example.org", "subject": "status?", "body_text": "hey, how is the run going", "attachments": [ { "filename": "report.pdf", "media_type": "application/pdf", "size_bytes": 48213, "disposition": "unscanned" } ] }

section.t: The normative shape is . Required members are contract_version, notice_id, and body_text; the rest — id, date, from, to, cc, subject, and attachments[] — is enrichment (). Descriptors here follow exactly the rules of , including the content_ref binding and the clean gating. This artifact's envelope is open, like the other Runtime-authored artifacts.

Resolution. A Connector's read surface resolves a notice identifier to a body from this artifact only, never from a provider fetch. The body is untrusted content, the same posture as the rest of message.

Enforcement by absence. A body the Runtime withholds — because of screening or quarantine, or because the message was never delivered — is simply not spooled, and a read against a missing artifact returns "not resolved." There is no other signal and no fallback fetch. The same "not resolved" response also covers an artifact the Runtime later removes under its own retention policy (): from the Connector's side, retired and never-spooled are indistinguishable, and both are already-specified behavior.

section.name: Task Correlation
section.t: The Runtime mints and owns task_id; a Connector only reads it, to correlate a Notice with prior work. The minting and thread-resolution algorithm is Runtime policy and out of scope. This protocol fixes three security obligations on it.

list.t: task_id MUST be unguessable and Runtime-minted — an HMAC over the thread root, for instance. It MUST NOT be a sequential or otherwise guessable value, and it MUST NOT be a capability an inbound sender can assert. (A guessable, sequential task_id was a confirmed exploit path in an early implementation.)

Matching a task_id, by itself, MUST NOT grant a message entry into that task. Authoritative correlation is header threading plus per-message verified sender identity. A subaddress or header token supplied by an inbound sender is a hint only, never authoritative: it is attacker-controllable, and it is stripped by many gateways.
Threading grants correlation, not trust. A message that threads onto a known task is still identity-verified per message; it does not inherit the task's standing.

section.name: Binding Record
section.t: The Binding Record is written by the Runtime or provisioner at the Volume root — <volume-root>/identity.json, a sibling of <agent-id>/, not inside it — and names which mailbox this Volume is bound to. Its normative shape is .
The Binding Record names which mailbox a Volume is bound to; it is informational and never consulted for enforcement (Section 9).

figure.title: fixtures/valid/identity-basic.json

list.t: Informational, not authoritative. The Volume is an Agent-writable filesystem, so a compromised Agent can edit or delete this file at will. Attribution and policy stay keyed on Runtime-side configuration (). This record grants nothing and is never consulted for enforcement.
Consumers MUST tolerate its absence, and MUST treat its contents as untrusted data: a malformed, oversized, or hostile file MUST never crash a reader or otherwise affect protocol behavior.

Its jobs are narrow by design: operator sanity — a human confirming which mailbox a Volume is bound to — a pre-start conflict check for whatever wrote it, catching for instance one Agent's credentials pointed at another Agent's Volume, and letting a Connector surface the Agent's own address back to its Agent.
The file is OPTIONAL (): nothing in this protocol requires a Runtime to write it or a Connector to read it, and both sides MUST work correctly with it absent.

Required members, if the file is present, are agent_id, address, and provisioned_ts. label is OPTIONAL. contract_version is OPTIONAL here — the one artifact where it is — because the file is not a protocol artifact a consumer must parse to function; if present it is pinned to "2".

This artifact's envelope is closed (additionalProperties: false), for a different reason than the Submit Request's is: closure here is an anti-secret-leak lint, catching a provisioner that writes credential material into a file living on an Agent-readable Volume. It is not a compatibility surface.

section.name: The Peer Directory
section.t: A Runtime MAY publish, at the Agent's Namespace root (<agent-id>/directory.json, beside the lanes rather than inside one), a per-instance projection of the authorisation graph naming which peers that Agent may address.

figure.title: draft/examples/directory.json (illustrative — not a fixture)

list.t: Advisory, never authoritative. The directory is the Runtime's most recent word about the graph, and grants nothing. A Connector MUST NOT treat an address's presence as a prediction that a submission to it will be accepted, nor its absence as a prediction of refusal: authorisation is evaluated by the Runtime at submission time, and the Result () is the only thing that reports what happened. A consumer that reads the directory as a prediction is wrong even when the file is current.

A Runtime MUST NOT read directory.json back, for any purpose. It is write-only from the Runtime's side: the graph is derived from policy, the file is a projection of the graph, and nothing derives the graph from the file. Enforcement remains the Runtime's own check against its graph, on every message. The prohibition is on the direction rather than the purpose, because the ways this decays — as an optimisation, a cache, a recovery source, or a cross-check — all have innocent intent, and the last two turn a projection into a source. A projection that can be read back becomes a cache; a cache becomes a record; a record that disagrees with policy wins by accident.

Per-instance projection. Each Agent's directory carries only the edges that Agent is party to. It MUST NOT carry the set of peers who may address that Agent, which is an allowlist in all but name, and MUST NOT carry the Agent's own address — attribution is the Namespace a file arrived in (), so an address an Agent reads is a claim rather than an identity.
router is the publishing Runtime's own address and MUST NOT appear in either list. Every address is one bare addr-spec ().
Both lists are always present, and empty when that lane is closed for this Agent; mail_to is empty in a delegation-only deployment. Absent and empty MUST NOT be conflated.
Written whole and atomically. A Runtime MUST NOT publish a newly adopted instance's address to others before it has adopted that instance itself.

A Runtime that publishes the directory MUST ensure the Agent can read it, and SHOULD expose it read-only. Publishing to a path the Agent's Namespace does not expose is not conformant: the write succeeds, the file is correct, and no Agent can read it — a failure that reports nothing on either side. Publishing is optional, so a Runtime that cannot make the file readable MUST NOT publish it; an unreadable directory is indistinguishable from an absent one to a consumer, and worse than an absent one to an operator, who has a file on disk that looks like it is working. The trap follows from the location: the file deliberately belongs to no lane, which is what keeps a delegation-only deployment from materialising a mail tree, and is exactly what places it outside an exposure built lane by lane.
written_at is the only staleness signal a consumer gets: an honest marker, not a freshness guarantee.

Where the consumer is an Agent rather than a parser, these become obligations to convey. A Connector that surfaces the directory to its Agent instead of interpreting it satisfies the obligations above by stating them, under the presentation rule in : the Agent is the party forming a belief, so the Connector MUST convey that an address's presence is not a prediction of acceptance, that the file may be absent, that an empty list and an absent list differ, and that written_at is the only staleness signal there is. A Connector with no directory parser does not thereby satisfy them vacuously.

The file MAY be absent — before first adoption, on a Runtime that does not implement this section, or after a failed write — and a consumer MUST tolerate absence exactly as it tolerates a missing Binding Record ().

A Runtime that cannot write it keeps routing. The directory is advisory, so a failed write loses a convenience, not the ability to enforce; failing closed would convert an advisory artifact into a dependency. The Runtime MUST log the failure. The Agent's only signal remains written_at going stale.

section.name: Versioning
section.t: The fail-closed rule. contract_version is a major-version string. A consumer that reads a higher major than it speaks MUST fail closed — refuse to process the artifact — and MUST NOT silently mis-parse it.

Version-check ordering. A consumer MUST implement the version check by reading contract_version before any schema validation, comparing majors as non-negative decimal integers. An absent major, a lower major, or a higher major is a version refusal: fail closed, as a distinct, logged outcome, never folded into the malformed-document drop path of .

Checking the version first is what makes fail-closed implementable at all. A validator that runs schema checks first cannot distinguish "wrong version" from "malformed," and a strict schema would reject a future-major document for the wrong reason entirely.

This ordering rule is about inbound artifacts a Connector consumes, which have no mechanism in this protocol to carry a distinct outcome back to the Runtime. It does not reach the outbound direction: a Runtime version-refusing a Submit Request MAY carry that refusal on the ordinary request-rejection path — a top-level rejected Result with reason_code: "unsupported_contract_version" () — and, per the conformance classes below, MUST do so for the version-absent request fixture. That is still a distinct, legible outcome rather than a fold into the malformed-request case: reason_code is exactly this protocol's mechanism for saying why a rejected fired, and a consumer MUST already tolerate a reason_code it does not otherwise interpret. A Runtime has no equivalent document to write for a version-refused Notice it never emits — hence the asymmetry: logged-only inbound, rejected outbound.

Why a version signal, rather than unknown-member rejection, is the boundary. At the transition from wire major "1" to "2", when attachment support was added, every top-level schema and every nested object except verdict and attestation.claims was additionalProperties: false. Under that regime, adding a member is not a safe additive change the way it would be under a permissive envelope: a strict major-1 validator rejects the whole document, not just the new member. Inbound, that is silent total message loss — an attachment-bearing email vanishes instead of degrading. Outbound, it is an accidental schema error rather than a designed refusal. And there is no signal to gate on while contract_version stays "1", because the new member is invisible to anything that would need to react to it. That is why attachments required a major bump: a major-1 consumer receiving a "2" document hits fail-closed by version, a legible and designed refusal, and both sides upgrade deliberately.

Explicitly deleted from this protocol's reasoning: any framing in which additionalProperties: false rejection is the version boundary. That conflates two different axes — schema strictness and protocol version — and produces catastrophic behavior (whole-document loss) exactly where a version check should produce a legible refusal.
Unknown-member tolerance is direction-aware. This is the rule that repairs the versioning model, and it is stated per direction because the two directions have opposite threat models.

list.t: Runtime-authored artifacts — Deliver Notice, Inbound Message, Result — are open. A consumer MUST ignore members it does not recognize, at every level of the document, and MUST NOT reject, drop, or fail the artifact on their account. Strictness on this direction defended nothing: the producer is trusted by construction, and in the one posture where an attacker can author a Notice — a writable inbound tree — that attacker can author a fully schema-valid one, so strictness was never the defense there. Its failure mode was silent mail loss. Emitting an unknown member remains a producer non-conformance: a Runtime MUST NOT emit members undefined at the version it claims. In the schemas, additionalProperties: false is absent from the deliver-notice, inbound-message, and result schemas at every level — top level, message, Descriptor items, and attestation — while the clean-gating conditionals are orthogonal and remain.

The Submit Request envelope stays closed, additionalProperties: false at every level. Closure is doing real security work there: it is what bars an outbound content_ref and any other smuggled member; the validator is the trusted Runtime; and a refusal is a legible, per-request rejected Result, never a silent loss. A Runtime MUST reject a request carrying unrecognized members.
Consequently: adding an optional member to a Runtime-authored artifact is genuinely additive and is a minor change; adding any member to the Submit Request is a major change.
The Binding Record is unchanged on this axis and stays closed for the separate reason given in .

section.t: Tolerance extends to values, not only members. An optional, explicitly advisory enum on a Runtime-authored artifact — message.sender_standing and message.provenance () — is scoped the same way. A consumer MUST tolerate a value it does not recognize, treating it as opaque or as the member being absent, and MUST NOT reject, drop, or fail the artifact on that account; a Runtime MAY add a value to either vocabulary as a minor change. This closes the same failure mode one indirection over: without it, a Runtime adding a fifth sender_standing or a third provenance value would silently lose every Notice carrying it, against every Connector still validating the old enum — identical to the member case, just at the value level. In the schemas, the enum constraint is absent from these two members.

This is not a universal loosening of every enum. kind, outcome — both the top-level Result outcome and the per-attachment outcome — and the inbound Descriptor's disposition remain closed, enum-locked vocabularies. kind and outcome gate which processing path a document takes at all, and disposition gates byte publication (), so a new value in any of them is a behavioral fork a consumer cannot safely treat as opaque. Introducing one is a major change.

Two version axes, allowed to diverge. The wire major tracks whole-document acceptance compatibility. The document version tracks the fuller set of obligations, including narrower, disclosed producer-side tightenings that do not rise to that level. Document version 3.0.0 is a major document bump — it moves fixtures between the valid and invalid sets, and it adds Runtime obligations a strictly-compliant earlier implementation does not meet — while the wire major stays "2".

Document version 3.1.0 (DRAFT) is an additive minor bump over 3.0.0; the wire major stays "2". It introduces the outbound extension space and its one normative clarification (, ), and the peer-origin profile's schema and conformance fixtures (, ). No existing schema rule or fixture changed. The profile's prose is a companion document not yet drafted; until it is, the schema and the peer-* fixtures are normative for the shape of a peer notice, and this document specifies nothing about the peer/ tree beyond that shape.

The reasoning for holding the wire major is worth stating, because the alternative is tempting and wrong. The wire major exists to force a legible fail-closed refusal when a whole document that a counterpart already accepts would otherwise be silently misread or silently dropped — the catastrophic, undetectable failure mode a version bump exists to convert into a designed refusal. Document version 3.0.0 does not claim that producer bytes are unchanged; they are not, on both sides (see the change log). But neither narrowing is that failure mode: each travels a designed, legible, per-artifact refusal path this protocol has always sanctioned, rather than a whole-document rejection triggered by an unrelated member. The Submit Request tightening yields a per-request rejected Result; the notice_id character-set tightening yields a per-Notice Connector-side drop under check 1 of — a real cost, disclosed in the change log, but a narrow and legible one, not silent total loss. Bumping the wire major to "3" would instead force every major-2 counterpart on both sides to refuse all traffic outright, including all the traffic the tolerance rule newly protects — inflicting exactly the catastrophic, undisclosed mail loss this version exists to repair, in order to fix incompatibilities that already have narrower, disclosed failure paths.

Corrections. Two claims that shipped in earlier revisions of this protocol's normative text were false, and are named here rather than quietly replaced, because an implementer who read them may have built against them.

list.t: The write-rule "strengthening" that was a regression. An earlier revision described the exclusive-create and no-symlink-follow requirement on the final path component as having been "strengthened to" the pinned directory-descriptor walk — that is, replaced by it — and deleted the earlier clause outright. That was a weakening, not a strengthening: a parent chain pinned by descriptor is silent about the final .tmp filename itself, so dropping exclusive-create there let an Agent that pre-plants a symlink at a predictable .tmp name have the Runtime write through it. now states the rule conjunctively, with all three legs required together.

The drop rule described as a closure over schema validation. An earlier revision described the inbound drop rule as a pure closure over schema validation, and claimed that formulation was exact against the fixture set. Both statements were false: the content_ref index and prefix binding is not expressible in the schema dialect used here, and a fixture exists that is schema-valid on its own and must nonetheless be dropped. now states two independent checks, and so does the Connector conformance class below.

section.t: A third correction concerns this protocol's own change history rather than an obligation, and is recorded in the change log: the document version that introduced message.provenance was labelled an additive minor change, which was unsound against the strictly-validating consumers of the time. The change log states what actually happened rather than relabelling the history.

Change control. A capability change starts with a change to this document, its schemas, and its fixtures, before either side implements it. Neither a Runtime nor a Connector may invent a wire member locally. Additive and backward-compatible changes are minor bumps; any change that breaks an existing fixture is a major bump, taken deliberately by both sides.

section.name: Required versus optional
section.t: contract_version is REQUIRED on every protocol artifact — Submit Request, Deliver Notice, and Result — with the Binding Record as the single exception (). The rest of this table reflects what implementations emit today; specified-but-unbuilt enrichment stays optional, and tightening any of it to required would be a future major bump.

c.spanx: contract_version, notice_id, ts, kind, message{id, from, subject, preview, mailbox}

texttable.c: message.{task_id, thread_id, in_reply_to, references, sender_standing, verdict, provenance}, message.attachments[] (items require filename, media_type, size_bytes, disposition; sha256 and content_ref optional, gated to disposition == "clean")
agent_id, ts, in_reply_to, draft.{cc, reply_to_message_id}, draft.attachments[] (items require filename, media_type, size_bytes, sha256)
detail, reason_code, ts, recipients, message_id, job_id, attestation (requires form; token and claims optional), attachments[] (items require index, outcome)
(the artifact itself is OPTIONAL — ); if present: contract_version, notice_id, body_text
id, date, from, to, cc, subject, attachments[] (same Descriptor rules as deliver-notice)
