label; contract_version (optional — if present, pinned to "2")

section.t: inbound/notices/processed/ is an OPTIONAL directory convention (), not a protocol artifact: it carries no schema, and no fixture exists or is needed for it.
Emission of contract_version on the three protocol artifacts is mandatory. An implementation not yet emitting it has an implementation conformance gap, not a license from this document.

section.name: Conformance
section.t: The fixtures are the other side. fixtures/ holds golden artifacts, and a producer or consumer proves conformance by passing them with no counterpart present (). That is what makes independent implementation practical: neither side needs the other to exist in order to demonstrate conformance.

Not every obligation in this document is wire-shaped. A behavioral obligation — one about how an implementation acts against a filesystem, rather than about the shape of a document — lies outside the fixture gate by construction and is checked operationally instead. lists every obligation of this kind that a green run does not prove.

This document defines two conformance classes. An implementation MAY claim both. Claiming either without the corresponding fixture run, and without the prescribed operational check for that class's behavioral obligations, is not conformance.
Runtime conformance class. An implementation claiming Runtime conformance:

list.t: MUST produce Deliver Notice documents valid against the deliver-notice schema () and Result documents valid against the result schema (); MAY produce Inbound Message documents, which when produced MUST be valid against the inbound-message schema (); and MAY produce a Binding Record valid against the binding-record schema ().
MUST consume Submit Request documents: it MUST accept every valid request-* fixture and MUST reject every invalid request-* fixture.

MUST demonstrate its producing side by confirming that its own emitted Notices, Results, and Inbound Messages satisfy the same schemas the suite's valid notice-*, result-*, and message-* fixtures satisfy — including the three fixtures carrying unrecognized members. A Runtime MUST NOT itself emit unrecognized members, but its parser, exercised by those fixtures, is what a Connector conformance run depends on it never having to special-case. It MUST also confirm that any Binding Record it writes satisfies the valid identity-* shape.

MUST uphold the filesystem and policy obligations of Sections through that no document validator can observe. lists them explicitly as what a green fixture run does not prove, and they are obligations of the class regardless — write-side path discipline (the conjunctive parent-chain-pinning, no-follow-while-building, and non-following-final-component rule), ingest by copy, read-side open discipline, and single-writer/single-drainer chief among them.

section.t: Connector conformance class. An implementation claiming Connector conformance:

list.t: MUST produce Submit Request documents valid against the submit-request schema (), and MUST NOT emit an outbound content_ref ().

MUST consume Deliver Notice, Inbound Message, and Result documents: it MUST accept every valid notice-*, message-*, and result-* fixture — including those carrying unrecognized members or unrecognized advisory-enum values — and MUST reject, meaning drop rather than surface, every invalid notice-* fixture except the version-refusal one, which it MUST instead refuse via the distinct version-refusal path (): never folded into the drop path, and never surfaced to the Agent either. 's drop rule is two independent conditions, not a closure over schema validation. "Fails schema validation for any reason other than an unrecognized member" (check 1) covers ten of the eleven other invalid notice-* fixtures — missing-required-member, wrong-kind, enum, pattern, and conditional violations alike. The eleventh is schema-valid on its own, producing zero errors from the gate's schema validator, and is caught only by the content_ref index and prefix binding (check 2, ), a named post-check the schema cannot express. A Connector conformance claim requires running both checks; schema validation alone does not close this set. Accepting the clean-Descriptor fixture — a Descriptor asserted clean and carrying content_ref and sha256 — is part of this obligation, and acceptance means relaying the Notice, not fetching the bytes: a Connector that never dereferences content_ref satisfies it ().
MUST return "not resolved" for a body whose Inbound Message is absent, and MUST NOT attempt any fallback fetch ().
MUST tolerate a Binding Record that is absent, and MUST NOT crash or otherwise misbehave on one that is hostile or malformed ().
MUST NOT require write access anywhere under inbound/, demonstrated by the operational check below rather than by a fixture ().

MUST demonstrate its producing side by confirming that its own emitted requests satisfy the same schema the suite's valid request-* fixtures satisfy, and MUST uphold the write-ordering, atomicity, and read-discipline obligations of , which the fixtures cannot check.

section.t: Read-only inbound tolerance — the prescribed operational check. Run the Connector against an inbound tree it cannot write — a genuinely read-only mount, not merely cleared permission bits, since a same-uid Agent can change a mode it owns — and confirm that it starts, relays every pending Notice, resolves bodies, and submits outbound requests, without requiring any write under inbound/ to succeed.

section.name: Security Considerations
section.t: This section gathers the threats this protocol's obligations exist to address. It introduces no new mechanism: every requirement referenced here is stated normatively in Sections through . The organizing principle throughout is the invariant of — enforcement is Runtime-side, and no property depends on the Agent or its Connector behaving.

The threat actor assumed throughout is a fully compromised Agent with write access to its own Namespace, running as a uid that owns the files it creates, able to act concurrently with the Runtime, and able to observe or predict the filenames the Runtime is about to use.

section.name: Path authority and traversal
section.t: An identifier drawn from a file's contents MUST NOT name a write path (). An early implementation trusted a req_id member inside a request body to name the path its Result would be written to, which is a confirmed exploit: the Agent controls that member and could therefore direct a Runtime-privileged write anywhere the Runtime could reach. The obligation is that the Runtime derives identifiers from the validated filename, over a restricted character set, and re-derives every path from data it controls.

The same reasoning is why inbound Sidecar directories and the body spool are keyed on the Runtime-minted notice identifier rather than the provider message.id: the provider identifier is external, arbitrary, and not character-set-safe, and using one as a path component was itself a confirmed exploit path. The schemas pin notice_id and req_id to character sets that are safe as path components; message.id is deliberately unconstrained, because it is never used as one.

section.name: Symlinks, descriptors, and open discipline
section.t: A shared filesystem between a trusted and an untrusted party makes every path-based check racy. The Agent can replace any component of a path it owns with a symlink, at any moment, including between a Runtime's check and the Runtime's subsequent act.
states the write-side discipline as three conjunctive requirements, and the conjunction is the point: each leg closes a gap the other two leave open.

list.t: Pinning only the final component leaves the parent swappable, and rename and directory-creation calls have no no-follow flag at all — so a bare "do not follow symlinks on writes" rule is not sufficient.

Pinning the parent chain without refusing symlinks while acquiring it means the pinned descriptor may point at whatever the Agent planted before the Runtime opened it — including across a Runtime restart, when the chain is re-opened.

Pinning the whole chain correctly still says nothing about the final filename. Every Runtime-written filename in the layout tree is predictable or observable to the Agent, so a pre-planted symlink at that name receives the Runtime's write with the Runtime's privileges unless the final open refuses to follow it and, where the file is newly created, refuses to reuse an existing name at all (O_EXCL).

section.t: The append-only audit log is the one write with no .tmp sibling to lean on, and it is called out separately for two reasons. O_EXCL cannot apply to a file that legitimately already exists, so the final-component protection there is a no-follow, append-mode, non-blocking open plus an fstat through the resulting descriptor. The non-blocking part is load-bearing rather than a performance nicety: a no-follow flag does not apply to a FIFO, because a FIFO is not a symlink, and opening a FIFO for writing blocks until a reader appears. An Agent that plants a FIFO at that filename therefore stalls the Runtime's drain indefinitely — a denial of service that the exclusive-create branch happens to refuse for free, and that this branch must refuse explicitly.

The read side mirrors all of it (): per-component no-follow opens or an equivalently pinned walk, a non-blocking open, an fstat through the open descriptor rather than a pre-open stat (which is itself a race), refusal of a multiply-linked file, and enforced size and count caps. The caps are not optional hardening: the too_large Result value presumes one, and without them an Agent can present an unbounded Sidecar or an unbounded request and exhaust the Runtime.

section.name: Time-of-check to time-of-use, and ingest by copy
section.t: Even with every open performed correctly, validating a file in place and then using it is a race: the Agent can rewrite the bytes between the check and the use, so the document that passed policy is not necessarily the document that gets composed and sent. The obligation that closes this is ingest by copy () — the Runtime copies the request and every Sidecar into Runtime-private Staging outside the Volume, and validates, evaluates policy on, and composes exclusively from that private copy, never re-reading an Agent-writable path after a decision that depends on its content.

This is also what keeps the trust model honest. Without it, the property "the request the Runtime approved is the request the Runtime sent" would rest on the Connector not rewriting a published file — an Agent-side obligation carrying a Runtime-side safety property, which the invariant of forbids. With it, that Connector obligation is pure well-formedness: a Runtime MAY treat an observed post-publish change as malformed, but nothing depends on the Connector honoring it.

section.name: Concurrency
section.t: Every atomicity guarantee in this protocol — the .tmp-then-rename discipline, the commit sentinel, the derivation of req_id from the maximum of the pending, processed, and result sets — assumes a single writer and a single drainer per Namespace, and none of them provides mutual exclusion (). Two concurrent drains can deliver the same request twice; two concurrent writers can collide on a req_id and clobber a published request, producing a verdict that names a request that no longer exists as written. The exclusion mechanism lives outside this protocol, and an implementation that does not provide one is not conformant, because behavior under violation is unspecified rather than merely degraded.

section.name: Attribution spoofing
section.t: Attribution is the Namespace a file arrived in, never an identifier inside the file (). A compromised Agent can write any agent_id it likes into a request; the member exists only as a cross-check, and a Runtime MUST reject a mismatch rather than believe it. Structural isolation is what actually enforces this: a Connector scoped to its own Namespace cannot name another Agent's.

The Binding Record deserves the same skepticism from the other direction (). It sits on an Agent-writable Volume, so its contents are untrusted data, it grants nothing, and it is never consulted for enforcement.

section.name: Untrusted content
section.t: Inbound mail is an injection vector aimed at the Agent's reasoning, and this protocol's posture is that every sender-originated string is untrusted content: bodies, subjects, previews, threading references, sender display names, and attachment Descriptors alike ().
Two cases are worth restating because they are the ones most often assumed safe.

message.from is attacker-controlled display data. Its display-name half is chosen freely by the sender, so a value such as "security@yourbank.example <attacker@evil.example>" is entirely legal and renders convincingly. It MUST NOT be used for a trust decision or shown to a human or an Agent as verified identity. Verified sender identity is only ever what the Runtime summarizes into sender_standing and verdict.

An attachment filename is an injection payload. A Descriptor is metadata about a file the Agent may never receive the bytes of, and a clean Disposition asserts something about bytes, never about the truthfulness of the strings describing them. A quarantined file named to look like an instruction reaches the Agent's context intact even though its bytes were withheld. media_type is likewise a declaration, which is why policy is governed by the Runtime's own sniffing of the bytes rather than by the declared type.

verdict, sender_standing, and provenance are advisory metadata for routing and presentation. None of them is a license for an Agent to obey body content, and this document deliberately does not define what an Agent should do with a message — that is Connector and deployment policy.

section.name: Recipient policy and header injection
section.t: Recipient policy is the exfiltration boundary, and it is a Runtime decision (). The Agent's draft.to and draft.cc are requests, not instructions. Two obligations make the boundary mechanical rather than best-effort: the Runtime MUST evaluate policy over exactly the recipient set it will transmit to, and it MUST NOT transmit to any address not present in those members. Without the first, policy can be evaluated over a parse of the recipients that differs from the one used for transmission; without the second, a Runtime-side addition (a bcc, an archive address) escapes the evaluated set.

The narrow addr-spec profile exists to make the evaluation mechanical. Display names, address lists inside a single element, quoted local parts, comments, IP literals, and folding whitespace are precisely the forms that make "does this address match the allowlist" a parsing problem with divergent answers — the classic confusion in which one parser sees the allowlisted address and the transmitting parser sees the attacker's. The profile is deliberately narrower than for that reason, and the cost is disclosed: some legitimate addresses cannot be expressed at this version.

Header injection is the second half. Any Agent-authored string that reaches the composed message can attempt to introduce a header boundary with CR, LF, or NUL. The schema patterns are the first line of defense, but a Runtime MUST also reject or strip those characters at composition time, because a document can reach composition by a path where schema validation was bypassed upstream. The two fields most easily overlooked are the ones composed directly into headers rather than into a body or display context: reply_to_message_id, which becomes an In-Reply-To: header, and an attachment's media_type, which becomes a MIME part's Content-Type: . An earlier revision's schema coverage stopped at subject and filename and missed exactly these.

section.name: The outbound digest is not a trust boundary
section.t: sha256 on an outbound attachment Descriptor is computed by the Connector over bytes the Connector wrote (). The Agent controls both, so a matching digest proves only that the request is internally consistent. It catches corruption and interrupted writes; it authenticates nothing. A Runtime MUST NOT treat a digest match as evidence about the content's safety, and MUST apply its own policy — sniffing the bytes, applying type and size rules — to the staged copy regardless.
The inbound direction is weaker still and is labelled as such: inbound size_bytes is provider-declared and advisory, not Runtime-verified ().

section.name: Confirmation-oracle avoidance
section.t: Inbound metadata is gated so that withholding bytes does not become an information channel. sha256 on an inbound Descriptor is emitted only where the Runtime asserts clean (). Publishing a digest for a withheld attachment would let an Agent confirm whether a guessed file was the one quarantined — a confirmation oracle — while providing no integrity value at all, since the Agent has no bytes to check it against.
The same principle governs quarantined mail generally: it produces no Notice at all, rather than a Notice announcing that something was withheld.

section.name: Byte-absence and artifact-absence as the access gate
section.t: The access gate in this protocol is the absence of bytes, not a flag inside a document (). A Runtime MUST NOT place non-clean bytes in an Agent's Namespace; content_ref is the grant, and it exists only where bytes were published. An Agent that ignores every Disposition it is shown still cannot read what was never written.

The same shape appears for bodies: a withheld or never-delivered message is simply not spooled, and a read against a missing artifact returns "not resolved," with no fallback fetch available to the Connector (). Because retention may also remove an artifact (), "retired" and "never spooled" are indistinguishable from the Connector's side — which is a deliberate property, not an ambiguity to be resolved by a new signal.

The content_ref binding rules () close the corresponding path-confusion risk: a consumer derives the byte path from the enclosing notice_id and the array index rather than from the content_ref string, and refuses any reference that does not match the pinned pattern or points outside its own inbound tree. Otherwise a Descriptor could name another Notice's Sidecar directory — including one belonging to a different delivery whose bytes the Agent was never granted.

section.name: Fail-closed version handling, and the cost of tolerance
section.t: A consumer reading a higher major than it speaks fails closed, and the version check runs before schema validation so that "wrong version" and "malformed" remain distinguishable (). Folding the two together is how a protocol acquires silent, undiagnosable mail loss.

The unknown-member tolerance rule is direction-aware precisely because tolerance has a security cost in one direction and a safety benefit in the other. On Runtime-authored artifacts, strictness defended nothing — the producer is trusted, and an attacker able to author a Notice at all (a writable inbound tree) can author a schema-valid one — while its failure mode was silent mail loss. On the Agent-authored Submit Request, closure is doing real work: it is what makes an outbound content_ref, or any other smuggled member, a hard rejection rather than a member the Runtime might one day interpret. A Runtime therefore MUST keep rejecting unrecognized members inbound from an Agent, and its rejection is legible — a rejected Result — rather than silent.

The value-level tolerance is scoped to the two explicitly advisory vocabularies for the same reason: kind, outcome, and disposition gate processing paths and byte publication, and treating an unrecognized value in any of them as opaque would let a producer's new value silently select a consumer's default path.

section.name: Inbound integrity and the writability of the inbound tree
section.t: A read-only inbound mount is the mechanism that makes a delivered Notice unforgeable (). Permission bits alone do not achieve it: a same-uid Agent can change a mode it owns, so an inbound tree protected only by bits is writable by the attacker in practice. Deployments that leave inbound writable should understand what they are accepting — an Agent can then author a schema-valid Notice for mail that never arrived, or alter one that did.

This is also why the tolerance rule does not weaken the inbound direction: in the writable-inbound posture, the attacker's forgery is schema-valid anyway, so schema strictness was never the control. The control is the mount.

Correspondingly, a Connector MUST NOT require write access under inbound/, and consumption tracking is Connector-private state kept elsewhere (). A Connector that crashes on a read-only inbound tree is broken against any Runtime enforcing inbound integrity.

section.name: Retention, deletion, and lost verdicts
section.t: Deletion rights are named per artifact class () because an unnamed right becomes either unbounded growth or an accidental data-loss path. Two hazards are worth restating.
A Result deleted before it is read is a lost verdict. No signal in this protocol tells a Runtime that a Connector has read one, so Runtime-side retention SHOULD be age-based and generous.

Deletion interacts with req_id monotonicity. A Connector exercising its deletion rights in processed/ or results/ removes exactly the state from which the next req_id is derived, and MUST preserve monotonicity by other durable means. Symmetrically, a Runtime MUST NOT treat processed/ as durable state — for deduplication, for instance — because the Connector may delete there. The Runtime's own record of what it sent belongs outside this protocol entirely.

section.name: What is wire-verifiable, and what is a Runtime obligation
section.t: A green conformance run proves that documents have the right shape. It proves nothing about a filesystem. The following are Runtime or Connector obligations that no document validator can observe, and a reviewer assessing an implementation must check them another way ( lists them as the gate's own honesty statement):

list.t: Sidecar file existence, and the binding between an ordinal and a directory entry on disk.
Whether size_bytes and sha256 match the bytes actually on disk.
Display sanitization of filename, and its never-a-path invariant.
The keying of inbound Sidecar directories on the Runtime-minted notice identifier.
The location of Runtime-private Staging, outside the mounted Volume.
Write ordering and commit-sentinel atomicity.
Caps, allowlists, and quotas.
The absence of a spooled body for a quarantined or blocked message.
A Connector's tolerance of a read-only inbound tree.
Ingest by copy.
Write-side path discipline, in all three of its conjunctive legs.
Read-side open discipline.
Single writer and single drainer per Namespace.
Compose-time rejection or stripping of CR, LF, and NUL.

section.t: Two of these deserve emphasis as trust-model statements rather than as testing notes. First, disposition == "clean" is the Runtime's assertion, and this document deliberately does not specify the basis for it; a consumer that treats clean as a proof rather than as an assertion has misread the trust model. Second, this protocol cannot make a Runtime trustworthy — it can only ensure that everything the Agent contributes is inert until a Runtime acts on it, and that whatever the Runtime asserts is legible and attributable to the Runtime.

section.name: The extension space, and outcomes as claims
section.t: outbound/ext/<name>/ () is Connector-owned and Agent-writable, and this document specifies no shape for anything under it. Its <name> is a stable, opaque Connector id (), so a Runtime's out-of-band agreement with a Connector survives that Connector's repository being renamed. Nothing security-relevant may be built on it. Its first use, a per-Notice outcome file, is written by the receiving Agent's own uid and is therefore forgeable by construction: a receiving Agent can claim a delivery that did not happen, deny one that did, or suppress a refusal. An outcome is a statement by the receiving side about what it did with a Notice; a party MUST NOT treat an outcome as proof of delivery or of non-delivery, and the Runtime's own delivery record is authoritative over it. A Runtime that reads outcomes may let them change what a sender is told or what an operator sees; it MUST NOT let them change what its own record says happened. There is deliberately no inbound extension space, because an inbound tree is a Runtime assertion about origin () and a Connector cannot know what a vendor-named assertion means.

front.title: The JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) Data Interchange Format

abstract.t: JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) is a lightweight, text-based, language-independent data interchange format. It was derived from the ECMAScript Programming Language Standard. JSON defines a small set of formatting rules for the portable representation of structured data.

front.title: UTF-8, a transformation format of ISO 10646

abstract.t: ISO/IEC 10646-1 defines a large character set called the Universal Character Set (UCS) which encompasses most of the world's writing systems. The originally proposed encodings of the UCS, however, were not compatible with many current applications and protocols, and this has led to the development of UTF-8, the object of this memo. UTF-8 has the characteristic of preserving the full US-ASCII range, providing compatibility with file systems, parsers and other software that rely on US-ASCII values but are transparent to other values. This memo obsoletes and replaces RFC 2279.

section.name: Conformance Suite

t.em: (Normative for the classes of ; the honesty statement below is part of the specification.)

section.t: The suite consists of golden artifacts under fixtures/valid/ and fixtures/invalid/, plus a validator, fixtures/validate.py.
At this document version the suite contains 82 fixtures — 31 valid and 51 invalid.
Running it. The validator is stdlib-only and takes no arguments:

figure.sourcecode: python3 fixtures/validate.py

section.t: It exits 0 if and only if every fixture under valid/ passes and every fixture under invalid/ fails. It requires no counterpart, no network, and no dependency: the fixtures are the other side.

How a fixture is mapped to a schema. By filename prefix — request- to the submit-request schema, notice- to deliver-notice, result- to result, message- to inbound-message, identity- to binding-record, and peer- to peer-notice ().

What the validator checks. Schema validation in the JSON Schema 2020-12 dialect , over the subset of keywords these schemas use (type, const, enum, minLength, pattern, minItems, minimum, items, required, properties, additionalProperties, allOf, and a single if/then pair) — plus two named post-checks, neither expressible in standard JSON Schema:

list.t: the Result-side binding attachments[i].index == i, contiguous and unique over 0 through n-1 ();

the content_ref index and prefix binding on Notice, Inbound Message, and peer-notice documents: every Descriptor carrying content_ref must equal <notice_id>.attachments/<i> for its own array position i, binding both the trailing index and the leading prefix ().

section.t: A Connector conformance claim requires running both the schema validation and the second post-check, because exactly one invalid notice-* fixture — and its peer-* counterpart — is schema-valid on its own and is caught only by that post-check (, ).

A note on pattern anchoring, and a portability cost. Every schema pattern in this suite that ends in $ is written as (?!\n)$. The reason is that a bare $ matches before a single trailing newline in several widely used regex engines — Python's re, Java, and .NET among them — unlike the ECMA-262 dialect JSON Schema specifies. Since every one of these patterns exists to forbid exactly the control characters a permissive $ would let through at the end of a string, the lookahead closes that gap in the schemas themselves rather than in any one validator. Seven fixtures pin the trailing-newline case specifically, distinct from the CRLF fixtures, which embed \r\n and were already rejected even under a permissive engine.

The cost is disclosed rather than discovered: lookahead-less engines cannot compile these patterns at all. RE2 (Go's regexp), Rust's regex crate, and POSIX ERE reject (?! outright, so the three schemas carrying the guard fail to load rather than validating loosely. Those engines already treat $ as strict end-of-string and never had the gap, so an implementer on one of them should strip the lookahead — not add a check outside the pattern, which would be both unnecessary and not what breaks. The failure is loud (a compile error, never silent acceptance).
What a green run proves. That every document shape this protocol defines is accepted or rejected as specified, by an implementation's own parser, with no counterpart present.

What a green run does NOT prove. The following are filesystem and policy invariants that no document validator can observe. They are obligations of the conformance classes regardless (), and are checked operationally:

list.t: Sidecar file existence — an extra file, a missing file, or a directory present when the Descriptor array is empty or absent.
size_bytes and sha256 actually matching the bytes on disk.
filename display-sanitization, and the "never a path" invariant.
The binding between an ordinal and a directory entry on disk. The schema checks only the Descriptor array's own index member, not that directory entry N exists.
Inbound Sidecar directories keyed on the Runtime-minted notice identifier rather than the provider message.id.
The location of Runtime-private Staging, outside the mounted Volume.
Write ordering and commit-sentinel atomicity — Sidecars before req-<id>.json; .tmp plus rename.
Caps and allowlists — type allowlists, size caps, Volume quotas.
The absence of a spooled body for a quarantined or blocked message (enforcement by absence, ).

A Connector's tolerance of a read-only inbound/ tree. The prescribed check is operational, not a fixture: run the Connector against an inbound tree it cannot write and confirm that it starts, relays every pending Notice, resolves bodies, and submits outbound requests, without requiring any inbound write to succeed ().
Ingest by copy — validation, policy evaluation, and composition running over a Runtime-private snapshot taken before any of those steps, rather than re-reading an Agent-writable path ().

Write-side path discipline, all three conjunctive legs: full parent-chain resolution through pinned directory descriptors from the Namespace root; each directory component opened O_NOFOLLOW|O_DIRECTORY at the moment it is added to that chain; and the final component created O_EXCL and never followed, failing closed on EEXIST and ELOOP. Any one leg alone is a known-insufficient partial mitigation ().

Read-side open discipline — per-component no-symlink-follow opens, non-blocking opens, fstat-based regular-file verification through the open descriptor, and bounded reads and caps on every Agent-influenced path ().
Single writer and single drainer per Namespace — an operational and deployment invariant, such as an OS-level lock held for the process lifetime ().

Compose-time header-boundary stripping: even where the schemas' control-character patterns are bypassed upstream, the Runtime rejects or strips CR, LF, and NUL before composing the outbound message ().

The peer-origin profile's operational obligations (v3.1.0 DRAFT), none of them visible to a document validator: the write-authority partition — no component that admits messages from a transport not restricted to authorised peer senders holds write authority over peer/, and the prescribed check is a write attempt from inside the admitting component that must fail; intake isolation for shared-transport peer candidates, in a location that is neither inbound/ nor peer/ and unreachable from any Agent Namespace; verification placement in a component holding peer write authority that hashes body and attachment bytes itself; sender_exposure never sender-settable; a peer notice carrying in_reply_to only when the placing Runtime resolved it from its own record, an unresolvable key being refused rather than stripped; and at-most-once action by the Connector, with an ambiguous target held rather than fanned out.

section.t: Beyond these, the behavioral obligations of Sections and — the untrusted-content posture, the treatment of task_id as correlation rather than authorization, and the requirement that verified sender identity never be taken from message.from — sit outside the fixture gate entirely. They constrain what an implementation does with a valid document, which no document-level gate can see.

section.name: A Deferred Seam-Visible "Handled" Signal (Non-Normative)
section.t: This appendix is non-normative and is not in force at this document version. It records the reasoning behind a gap deliberately left open, not an addition to the protocol. Nothing below is a directory, a member, or an artifact that a conforming implementation can rely on, and no requirement keyword appears anywhere in it.

The gap. Making inbound consumption-tracking Connector-private () closes the writability conflict but leaves a knowledge and capability split unbridged: only the Connector knows that a Notice has been relayed to its Agent, while on a read-only inbound tree only the Runtime can delete anything. Neither side alone can turn "consumed" into "reclaimed."

A sketch, not a specification. One shape that would bridge it is a Connector-written, zero-byte marker per acknowledged Notice, written into outbound/, where the Connector already has write access in every posture:

figure.title: Sketch only — not part of this protocol
figure.sourcecode: outbound/acks/notice-<id> # sketch only - not part of the protocol

section.t: A Runtime could then delete the acknowledged Notice and its spooled message, and finally the marker itself. This is presented purely as a sketch: no directory and no wire member is introduced by this appendix.

Why a Connector-forgeable signal would be acceptable here. A garbage-collection signal is a resource decision rather than a security decision. An Agent that falsely claims consumption loses only its own unread mail; one that never claims consumption only bloats its own inbox. Neither crosses a trust boundary that matters, and neither touches any record of the exchange the Runtime keeps on its own side. That is what distinguishes this case from every other "the Agent writes it, so it cannot be trusted" case in this document — but it is a distinction a future version would need to state explicitly rather than assume.

Why a high-water mark cannot substitute. requires task_id to be unguessable and never sequential, and nothing in this document orders notice identifiers, so no single "processed through N" cursor is expressible. Any consumption signal has to be a set of identifiers, or time-ordered — and time-ordering would require the consumer to process strictly in delivery order, which nothing today requires.

The lifecycle this would enable, and its boundaries. A reliable "is this one done?" answer is the watermark a real retention lifecycle promotes against: cycling a working set, rolling handled traffic into period-compacted archives, then expiring or tiering to cold storage. Three boundaries would need to hold if this is ever specified.

list.t: The seam is not the record. A Runtime that needs an exchange of record already keeps one outside this protocol, tamper-evident. Retention here is about an Agent's access to its own history, not about the durability of evidence; conflating the two produces an archive that satisfies neither.

An Agent-writable archive is never evidence. A compacted archive living under outbound/, which is Agent-writable in every posture, can be rewritten by the Agent it belongs to. Anything meant to be relied on has to be Runtime-written or kept outside this protocol entirely.

It must not grow the read surface. The read available today is a point lookup from a notice identifier to a body. "Search my archive" is a materially larger capability — decompression, indexing, query — for a deliberately dumb, credential-free relay to take on. If archives are ever exposed to an Agent, that likely belongs behind a Runtime-served surface rather than the file-drop seam.

section.t: Why this is deferred rather than specified now. A capability starts with a change to this document once a second implementation independently wants it, with members and fixtures proposed together. Today exactly one reference Connector carries a private workaround for the underlying problem — a writability-probing fallback with three modes: move, ledger, and in-memory. There is no second data point yet to generalize from, and specifying now would freeze one side's convention as the protocol's answer.

One honesty note for a future implementer. The sketch's own garbage-collection step is not atomic: if a Runtime crashes between deleting the Notice artifacts and deleting the acknowledgment marker, the marker is orphaned, pointing at a Notice that no longer exists. Any real design needs idempotent collection, in which a missing target is not an error — recorded here so that it is not rediscovered from scratch.

t.em: (Informative. One entry per document version, newest first, derived from the versioning record of the protocol contract this document renders.)

section.name: 3.1.0 (DRAFT) — the protocol is AMAP; the outbound extension space; the peer-origin profile's schema
section.t: An additive minor bump; the wire major stays "2".

list.t: The protocol is AMAP; the schema $id authority is amap-spec (2026-09-15). The protocol formerly called AMP ("Agent Mailbox Protocol") is renamed AMAP ("Agent Mailbox Access Protocol") because AMP collides with the IETF DTN working group's adopted draft-ietf-dtn-amp; the specification repository moves from agent-mailbox-protocol to amap-spec with it. The six schema $id values move from https://agent-mailbox-protocol/schemas/… to https://amap-spec/schemas/…. Nothing on the wire changes shape: no document carries the protocol's name as a field, and $id is an identifier the gate never dereferences. Implementations that mirror the Runtime's address spell its local part amap.router from this version. This draft's filename is a separate decision and is unchanged here. This version is marked DRAFT: its profile prose is a companion document (spec/peer-origin.md, itself DRAFT), and its schema and fixtures may still change before it is settled.

Outbound extension space. outbound/ext/<name>/ is defined as a Connector-owned side channel a Runtime MAY read by out-of-band agreement, with no shape specified and nothing security-relevant permitted to depend on it (). <name> is pinned as a stable Connector id — chosen once, unchanged by any rename of the Connector's repository, package, or deployment, and opaque to the Runtime that reads it; the wording it replaced ("a Connector or deployment name") permitted a repository name to leak into a wire-visible path. The first id is claude-code. One normative clarification sits beside it: an outcome written there is a claim by the receiving side, never proof of delivery or of non-delivery, and the Runtime's own delivery record is authoritative over it (). There is deliberately no inbound extension space.

Peer-notice schema. The peer-origin profile's artifact is pinned by peer-notice.schema.json (): the deliver-notice layout with kind and mailbox fixed to peer, message.from a bare addr-spec, message identifiers in the notice-identifier character set, and the optional Runtime-asserted sender_exposure stamp with its required members. The profile's prose is the companion document spec/peer-origin.md (v3.1.0 DRAFT).

Fixtures: 75 total (27 valid, 48 invalid), up from 58. 16 peer-* fixtures were added (6 valid, 10 invalid), covering a minimal notice, a reply, the exposure stamp asserted both ways, a clean attachment reference, an unknown-member case, and rejections for a deliver kind under the peer tree, a peer kind under the inbound tree, a display-name or CRLF from, encoded message identifiers, a missing asserted_by, a missing last-delivery timestamp when exposure is asserted true, an inbox mailbox, a content_ref index mismatch, and a trailing-newline identifier. The validator maps the peer- prefix to the new schema and applies the content_ref post-check to it. Three existing fixtures had example strings normalised to example.* identities (one free-text body, two addresses in injection examples); each stays valid or invalid for the same reason as before, and no schema changed.

section.name: 3.0.0 — direction-aware tolerance, and six closed safety holes
section.t: A major document bump; the wire major stays "2". states why the two numbers diverge here, and why bumping the wire would have caused the exact harm this version exists to repair.

list.t: Unknown-member tolerance, direction-aware. The three Runtime-authored artifacts — deliver-notice, inbound-message, and result — became open at every level: additionalProperties: false was removed from the top level, from message, from Descriptor items, and from attestation, and a consumer must tolerate an unrecognized member. Emitting one remains producer non-conformance. The Agent-authored submit-request envelope stays closed at every level. Consequence: adding an optional member to a Runtime-authored artifact is now genuinely additive; adding any member to the submit-request is a major change.

...and for values. The enum constraint was removed from message.sender_standing and message.provenance, the two explicitly advisory vocabularies, and a consumer must tolerate an unrecognized value in either. kind, outcome (both levels), and disposition remain closed, enum-locked vocabularies.

Ingest by copy. A Runtime must copy an Agent-authored request and its Sidecars into private staging before validating, must act only on that copy, and must not re-read an Agent-writable path after a decision depending on its content ().

Address syntax and header-injection discipline. A new obligation in plus schema patterns on draft.to/cc, draft.subject, attachment filename and media_type, draft.reply_to_message_id, in_reply_to, agent_id, and ts — including the two members composed directly into headers, which earlier schema coverage missed.

Path discipline, write- and read-side both. The write-side rule became conjunctive (), and a new read-side rule applies the equivalent discipline to every Agent-influenceable read. A notice_id character-set pattern was added to the deliver-notice and inbound-message schemas so that every legal notice_id is also a legal content_ref prefix. Disclosed cost: notice_id was previously unconstrained, so a Runtime minting identifiers outside the new character set — an ISO-8601 timestamp, standard base64, a URN, or anything else carrying punctuation outside it — now emits Notices and Inbound Messages that fail schema validation on a pattern violation on a required member, and a conforming Connector drops them. Migration: such a Runtime must re-mint identifiers under the new character set (unpadded base64url or lowercase hex, for instance) before any Connector it talks to upgrades, because the failure is otherwise silent on both sides.
Single writer, single drainer. now names the concurrency assumption that every atomicity, commit-sentinel, and req_id rule already depended on.
message.from named untrusted. The untrusted-content sentence now covers explicitly the member most likely to be rendered to a human or used for a trust judgement ().

Document authority. The contract, its schemas, and its fixtures are normative; this rendering is generated from them and is non-authoritative where they disagree. The conformance-class text was moved into the contract itself so that the demotion deletes nothing, and a stray claim of a second, message-specific Sidecar directory was corrected to match the layout tree.

Corrections shipped with this version, rather than a tidied history: (i) the write rule described in an earlier revision as "strengthened" had in fact been weakened — the exclusive-create requirement on the final component had been deleted rather than supplemented (); (ii) the inbound drop rule described as a pure closure over schema validation was refuted by this version's own content_ref-binding fixture, and is now stated as two independent checks (, ); (iii) the claim that this version's producer bytes are unchanged is explicitly not made — two producer-side narrowings are disclosed above, each travelling a legible per-artifact refusal path; and (iv) the 2.1.0 entry below is corrected in place.

Fixtures: 58 total (21 valid, 37 invalid), up from 44. The unknown-member notice fixture moved from the invalid set to the valid set and was extended with an unrecognized member inside message; valid unknown-member fixtures were added for result and inbound-message; the withheld-body invalid fixture was deleted, having become schema-valid under the relaxed envelope (its name always over-claimed what additionalProperties alone tested); the bad-provenance fixture moved to the valid set as an unrecognized-value case; an invalid extra-member submit-request fixture was added to pin the closed side of the asymmetry, previously untested at the top level; four invalid fixtures were added for the address-syntax and control-character rules; a traversal notice_id fixture was added; the content_ref index-mismatch fixture was added, and is the one invalid notice-* case that is schema-valid on its own; and six fixtures pin the trailing-newline anchoring case.

section.name: 2.3.0 — inbound byte access in force
section.t: A minor bump, prose only: no schema rule and no fixture changed, and the wire major stayed "2". It resolved an inconsistency carried since 2.0.0. A fixture showing a clean Descriptor with content_ref and sha256 sat in the valid set as a deliberately forward-valid shape, while the prose forbade any Runtime from producing it — the gate blessed what the prose forbade. This version sided with the fixtures: the release-scoped byte embargo was dropped, and the standing rule became the one stated in — a Runtime may publish bytes and emit content_ref/sha256 only for a Descriptor it asserts clean, and a Runtime that cannot make that determination must not assert clean. The substantive clarification is that disposition is the Runtime's assertion, its basis deliberately unspecified; the older prose presumed a scanner, which is what made byte access read as a deferred capability rather than as a policy decision whose wire shape major 2 already carried. Nothing was tightened, and there is still no outbound content_ref.

section.name: 2.2.0 — deletion rights, read-only inbound
section.t: A permissive minor bump: no wire member, no schema change, no fixture changed or added. It (a) declared a read-only inbound tree a valid Runtime posture and made the inbound processed/ archive directory optional, (b) obliged a Connector not to require inbound write access, making consumption-recording Connector-private, and (c) named deletion rights per artifact class, along with the two constraints attached to them: a Connector must not delete or rewrite a published request, and a Connector exercising its new deletion rights must preserve req_id monotonicity by other durable means. It also pinned three previously implicit reason_code rules: setting one on every Result became a keyworded SHOULD, and a consumer must tolerate an unrecognized code and must not infer outcome from it.

section.name: 2.1.0 — the body spool, and three optional Result members
section.t: Recorded at the time as an additive minor bump: one new optional spooled artifact (the Inbound Message) and its schema, one new optional Notice member (provenance), and three new optional Result members (reason_code, attestation, ts). No existing schema gained a required member, no existing fixture changed shape, and the wire major stayed "2".

Correction (recorded at 3.0.0). That "additive minor" label was unsound as written. Against a strictly validating 2.0.0 consumer — every schema at that version was closed at every level — a Notice carrying the new provenance member failed schema validation as a whole document and was silently dropped: precisely the failure mode cited as the reason attachments had required a major bump, reintroduced as a minor. Version 3.0.0 repairs the versioning model rather than relabelling this history, which is why this entry still records what shipped rather than what would have been correct.

section.name: 2.0.0 — attachments, and contract_version required
section.t: A major bump, moving the wire major from "1" to "2". It added attachment support in both directions — outbound Descriptors with required size_bytes and sha256 and their Sidecar bytes, inbound Descriptors with a disposition — and made contract_version REQUIRED on the submit-request, deliver-notice, and result artifacts, with no compatibility mode. The reason the bump had to be major rather than minor is the reasoning in : under the then-universal closed envelopes, a new member caused a major-1 consumer to reject the whole document, which inbound is silent total message loss. A version signal, rather than an unknown-member rejection, is what makes that refusal legible.

section.name: Fixture identifier normalization
section.t: Across these versions the fixture suite's identities were normalized to example.com and example.org placeholders, and deployment-specific identifiers were removed from fixture content. This changed no shape and no expectation: every affected fixture validates exactly as before, and no identifier removed in that pass is reintroduced by this document.
